processing: No single style. Misho only says the bushes grew from Yabukita seed; one Sayama garden, for one, makes a black tea from such leaf.
harvest_season: Varies by maker, usually sold from a named spring picking; the known Sayama example is first flush.
appearance_dry: Depends on how it is made: dark green needles if sencha-style, as is typical, and dark twisted leaf as black tea.
appearance_liquor: Depends on how it is made: yellow-green as a steamed green, as is typical of Japanese greens.
appearance_wet: Soft green leaf pieces when made as a steamed green; plants may vary within a field.
taste_profile: No settled profile is on record. Seed-grown plants differ from one another, so expect it to vary by garden.

brewing.notes: Sencha settings for a green version. A black tea made from this leaf wants hotter water, around 90°C.

vintage_note: Sold in tiny lots by individual gardens, labelled by harvest and year where stated. As with other Japanese greens, green versions are best fresh from the current year's harvest.
description:
Yabukita Misho means Yabukita grown from seed. Yabukita proper is a clone, propagated by cuttings; a misho bush is a seedling of it, and the name marks that difference.

This matters because seedlings do not copy their parent. As with any seed-grown tea, a field can be less uniform than clonal rows. Breeders have used natural Yabukita seedlings as a pool of new cultivars for that very reason, including Yamakai.

Little is documented on how the tea itself tastes. The clearest example on the market is a first-flush black tea from a Sayama grower, which shows the label is about the plant and not a style.

So read the label for the maker and the processing, not just the name, and do not assume it will taste like a standard Yabukita sencha.
history: Little is documented about when growers began selling tea under this label. The term appears in Japanese cultivar lists as 薮北実生, and it describes a kind of plant, not a bred and named cultivar.
